title: How to invest in U.S. treasury bonds as a safe option
description: A step-by-step guide to buying T-Bills, Notes, and Bonds for risk-free income.
content:
When the stock market feels like a rollercoaster, investors flock to safety. In the financial world, the ultimate 'Safe Haven' is US Treasury debt. Backed by the 'full faith and credit' of the United States government, Treasuries are widely considered the risk-free benchmark for the entire global economy. Unlike savings accounts which can change rates daily, Treasuries allow you to lock in a guaranteed yield for a specific period—from 4 weeks to 30 years. This guide explains the mechanics of buying them and how to build a 'Bond Ladder' to protect your principal.

Key Takeaways

  • State Tax Free: One of the biggest perks. Interest earned on US Treasuries is exempt from state and local income taxes, boosting effective yield in high-tax states.
  • Duration Management: T-Bills (<1 year), T-Notes (2-10 years), and T-Bonds (20-30 years) behave differently. Short term is cash-like; long term is volatile.
  • Liquidity: Treasuries are highly liquid. You can sell them instantly on the secondary market through any major brokerage.
  • Yield Curve: Understanding inverted vs. normal yield curves helps you decide whether to lock in rates short-term or long-term.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Buying Treasuries used to be clunky via TreasuryDirect.gov. Today, most US brokerages (Fidelity/Schwab) allow you to buy them directly in your account with $0 commissions. This integration makes them a viable alternative to High-Yield Savings Accounts for parking cash.

The Treasury Menu

Not all government debt is the same. Choose the right vehicle for your timeline.

1. Treasury Bills (T-Bills)

  • Maturity: 4, 8, 13, 26, or 52 weeks.
  • How they pay: Sold at a discount. You pay $990, get back $1,000. The $10 is your interest.
  • Best For: Emergency funds, House down payments, Short-term cash parking.

2. Treasury Notes (T-Notes)

  • Maturity: 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years.
  • How they pay: Coupon payments every 6 months.
  • Best For: Locking in yield for medium-term goals. The '10-Year Treasury' is the benchmark for mortgage rates.

3. Treasury Bonds (T-Bonds)

  • Maturity: 20 or 30 years.
  • How they pay: Coupon payments every 6 months.
  • Risk Warning: These are volatile. If rates rise, the price of a 30-year bond crashes. Only for advanced hedgers.

How to Buy (Brokerage vs. TreasuryDirect)

  1. Method A: Brokerage (Recommended): Log into Fidelity/Schwab. Go to 'Fixed Income' -> 'New Issues'. You can buy T-Bills at auction. Advantage: You can sell them easily if you need cash early.
  2. Method B: TreasuryDirect.gov: The government's direct portal. Advantage: $100 minimums (vs $1,000 at brokers). Disadvantage: Terrible website, hard to sell, requires complex login security.
  3. The Auction Process: You place an order before the auction date. The rate is determined at auction (e.g., 4.5%). You don't know the exact rate until the auction closes, but it rarely surprises.
  4. Auto-Roll: Select 'Auto-Roll' to have your T-Bill automatically reinvested upon maturity. This creates a perpetual income machine.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I lose money on a T-Bill?

Only if you sell it early and interest rates have risen since you bought it. If you hold it until maturity (e.g., 3 months), you are guaranteed your full principal back.

Are I-Bonds the same thing?

No. Series I Savings Bonds are a special type of inflation-protected bond that you can only buy at TreasuryDirect. They have purchase limits ($10k/year) and cannot be traded.

Why buy a 10-Year Note if cash pays more?

In 2025, cash might pay 5% and 10-Year Notes pay 4% (Inverted Curve). Investors buy the 10-Year to lock in 4% for a decade, betting that cash rates will drop to 2% soon.
